item.title: Bot traffic versus human traffic — who will win this battle?
item.description:
The idea of the so-called "dead internet" has been floating around for quite some time (if memory serves, there were tentative statements in support of this theory as early as 2014), but every year the voices of those who consider it real grow louder. And indeed, the development of AI, automation, and resource parsing contributes to the flooding of the internet with bots. But is everything as critical as it seems at first glance?

We decided to examine what is happening in the modern internet in terms of human and bot traffic, and to figure out whether the "dead internet" is really that close, or if it still resembles a conspiracy theory.

What has become of the internet?

item.title: [Translation] Because of AI, I've become lazy. Or have I been a lazy person for a long time, and now it's become impossible to hide it?
item.description:
Should you stop using AI right now?

I hate AI tools. Which is pretty funny because I literally make a living building AI automations. That's my job. But recently I experienced something that made me completely rethink my relationship with these tools. I lost my sense of purpose, lost interest in work, and for a long time couldn't understand why. Then I accidentally watched a video about a Greek word I had never heard before — and finally understood what was happening.

item.title: Entry into SpecDriven Development: OpenSpec vs SpecKit
item.description:
Agents write code faster than any human can review it — so the knowledge that used to be stored in developers' heads must now live somewhere else.

A practical analysis of two key approaches to spec-driven development: how their workflows work, how extensible they are, and in which places both OpenSpec and Spec Kit still leave you one-on-one with the agent.

item.title: Code review in the era of AI: 7 mistakes leading to incidents
item.description:
AI can already generate hundreds of lines of code in minutes, but the speed of review has not increased from this. We analyze seven errors due to which AI Code Review misses real defects, creates a false sense of security, and gradually turns code review into a formality.

Break down the errors

item.title: How much will the collapse of artificial intelligence cost?
item.description:
In May, 17% of the total growth of the entire global stock market came from just two companies — Micron and SK Hynix, manufacturers of memory chips. Not 17% of the semiconductor sector's growth, but 17% of the entire market — that is, all publicly traded companies in all countries combined. These figures are cited by Acadian Asset Management. In the company's report, the global market refers to the MSCI All Country World Index, which includes thousands of stocks from dozens of countries. Meanwhile, Micron and SK Hynix together account for about 1% of that index. In other words, out of every dollar the global market gained in May, roughly 17 cents came from just these two stocks.

This raises an uncomfortable question: if the entire global stock market can be lifted by the shares of just two chipmakers that most people have never even heard of (we're not talking about Apple or Google here), what will happen to your portfolio when the market turns downward?

So today, we'll explore how much ordinary investors are tied to the bet on artificial intelligence, why the usual safe havens may not provide protection, and roughly how much money could disappear if this entire structure collapses.

Read more

item.title: I've had enough of VPNs that keep dropping: how I once and for all solved the issue of accessing ChatGPT from Russia.
item.description:
On Thursday I stayed up late working on a task and was counting on ChatGPT's help to finish faster. I open the chat — oh, hello, "This model's response is unavailable." The VPN, which had been working faithfully for half a year, decided to go down at that exact moment. Restart, switch servers, another restart — thirty wasted minutes and a task that I had to finish by three in the morning.

The next day I sat down to figure out how to make sure this never happened again. 

I took a stand: never, and I mean NEVER again would I lose access to ChatGPT because of a VPN. An OpenAI server error, the lights going out at home, a meteorite hitting the system unit — okay, I'm powerless against those. But a broken VPN will no longer be an obstacle for me.

What I ended up with is a rather clunky and inconvenient workaround, but it works. If you happen to be reading this text in the same situation I was in on Thursday, I'd be happy to help.

Read more

item.title: Claude Code Antifraud, Part 2: Bisector Rats and Median Monkeys at a Children's Mathematical Olympiad
item.description:
In the previous episode, a friend brought me an imported one for three hundred and asked me to check the results of the Moscow Geometry Olympiad. While I was publishing the article, a second order came in. This time it's the St. Petersburg Olympiad for grades 4–11: 6 seasons, 40+ venues, oral format. Oral means the participant explains the solution, the jury nods or doesn't nod, no drafts, no double-checking.

And again, an imported one for three hundred. Well, three hundred it is. Let's go.

Read more

item.title: "RAG system for analyzing news from the perspective of a historical figure based on literary sources 'AI_Lenin'"
item.description:
The widespread presence of mass media on the internet has led to the formation of a group of thematic experts — opinion leaders — bloggers. Their task is to evaluate and analyze facts, presenting information through the prism of their own opinion.

Naturally, this prompts a mental exercise: how would a person who left a mark on history assess one or another modern fact?

Read more

item.title: Xiaomi AI Cube — everything that is known about the AI computer on three XRing chips.
item.description:
In mid-August 2026, details emerged in China's closed segment about a private showcase of Xiaomi's silicon division. The company brought a working engineering prototype called the Xiaomi AI Cube.

And this is no longer just another NUC on an Intel or AMD mobile processor. What we have here is a compact workstation built specifically for a very concrete task: running open-source neural networks locally, with up to 120 billion parameters, without connecting to the cloud and without Nvidia graphics cards.

Read more

item.title: You are implementing AI incorrectly and what is context debt.
item.description:
An AI agent can be assembled in just a few hours today. But that doesn't mean businesses understand where it should actually be implemented.

Companies often start with Build: they choose a model, integrate Jira, GitHub, MCP, and put together a workflow. Only afterward do they try to figure out what problem they actually solved.

In this article, I analyze a different approach: first, identify where the team loses time on context restoration, manual coordination, and switching between systems. To do this, we use Context Audit and the concept of context debt.

We'll discuss how to spot such problems in Jira, Confluence, and GitHub, why not every one of them should be automated, and what to do after the audit.

Read more

item.title: "He is 10 out of 10, but...": Discussed the pitfalls of implementing AI agents at the True Tech Friends festival.
item.description:
Today, companies are increasingly using neural networks not only for individual queries, but also for executing entire chains of tasks. An AI agent can independently find information, write code, access an internal system, and prepare a result. The more such actions the system performs without human involvement, the more important control over its work becomes, and the higher the cost of an error.

At the third True Tech Friends festival, experts discussed real cases of implementing AI agents and situations where automation began to work differently than expected. The discussion centered on a practical question: where does an agent truly need autonomy, and which tasks are better left to conventional algorithms.

The discussion involved Yaroslav Losev, head of the frontend development team at Yandex Travel; Sergey Kurbanov, head of research and development at MWS; and Daniil Slyusar, head of development for PT Application Inspector at Positive Technologies.

Read more

item.title: Sergey Brin: from Moscow emigrant to creator of Google
item.description:
On Friday, August 21, billionaire Sergey Brin turned 53. He is known as the co-founder of Google. According to Forbes, in 2026 Brin's net worth is estimated at $260 billion, making him the fourth richest person in the world.

Brin's story stands out among other ultra-wealthy entrepreneurs, as he became the most successful business and technology figure to come from the USSR.

Read more

item.title: The application crashed in a closed loop: hidden downloads in Python libraries for ML
item.description:
My name is Pavel, I am a developer at R77.AI. In this article, I will explain why Python libraries for ML can secretly access the internet, how to find such hidden downloads, and what to do about them in a closed-loop environment.

Read more

item.title: "One nip carefully zamifril", or how linguists analyze language inside LLMs
item.description:
No matter what the LLM does. The task still comes in words, and a single missing not can ruin an already quite tangible action. I look at the LLM through the eyes of a linguist and figure out how a language scholar tests an LLM from tokenization to pragmatics, and what a developer can turn from this philological pedantry into code, metrics, and tests.

Read more

item.title: Half of the work for which I became a programmer is now done by an agent. What's next?
item.description:
The profession is changing before our eyes: part of the work that once brought us to code and was a pleasure is now shifting under the responsibility of LLMs. We are still engineers — we read code, we maintain architecture — but let's be honest, this is already a different profession.

The question that haunts me is: how can those of us with years of experience continue to grow in this new world — where do we learn new ways of working with AI, and where do we put our own discoveries? I've come to argue and gather your opinions.

Read more
